source_text: Habet christianus spectacula meliora, si uelit, habet ueras et profuturas uoluptates, si se recollegerit: et ut omittam illa quae nondum contemplari potest, habet istam mundi pulcritudinem quam uideat atque miretur, solis ortum aspiciat, rursus occasum mutuis uicibus dies noctesque reuocantem, globum lunae temporum cursus incrementis suis detrimentisque signantem, astrorum micantes choros et assidue de summa mobilitate fulgentes, anni totius per uices membra diuisa et dies ipsos cum noctibus per horarum spatia digestos et terrae molem libratam cum montibus et profusa flumina cum suis fontibus, extensa maria cum suis fluctibus atque litoribus, interim constantem pariter summa conspiratione nexibusque concordiae extensum aerem medium tenuitate sua cuncta uegetantem, nunc imbres contractis nubibus profundentem, nunc serenitatem refecta raritate reuocantem et in omnibus istis incolas proprios, in aere auem, in aquis piscem, in terra hominem. haec, inquam, et alia item opera diuina sint christianis fidelibus spectacula. quod theatrum humanis manibus exstructum istis operibus poterit comparari? magnis licet lapidum molibus exstruatur, cristae sunt montium altiores, et auro licet tecta laquearia reluceant, astrorum fulgore uincentur: numquam humana opera mirabitur quisquis se recognouerit filium Dei. deicit se de culmine generositatis suae qui admirari aliquid post Deum potest.
thought_title: The Christian's better shows: creation as spectacle
orientation: Novatian, the author, is addressing faithful Christians and has just begun the work; here he turns from the forbidden public shows to the better shows that Christians already possess in the beauty of the created world.
pass_a_gloss: A Christian has better public shows, if he is willing, he has true and beneficial pleasures, if he recollects himself: and to pass over those things which he is not yet able to contemplate, he has this beauty of the world which he may see and admire, he may look at the rising of the sun, and again its setting recalling days and nights by mutual turns, the globe of the moon marking the courses of the seasons by its increases and its decreases, the glittering choirs of the stars and constantly shining from their highest mobility, the limbs of the whole year divided through their turns and the days themselves with the nights arranged through the spaces of the hours and the mass of the earth balanced with its mountains and the pouring rivers with their springs, the stretched-out seas with their waves and shores, meanwhile the air stretched out in the middle, equally constant by the highest harmony and by the bonds of concord, quickening all things by its thinness, now pouring out rains from gathered clouds, now recalling clear weather by restored openness, and in all these things its own inhabitants, in the air the bird, in the waters the fish, on the earth man. These things, I say, and other works of God likewise are public shows for faithful Christians. What theater built by human hands will be able to be compared with these works? Although it is built with great masses of stone, the crests of the mountains are higher, and although the paneled ceilings gleam with gold, they will be surpassed by the brightness of the stars: never will anyone admire human works who has recognized himself as a son of God. He casts himself down from the height of his nobility who is able to admire anything after God.

choices.why: Keeps the glossary term 'public shows' for spectacula and preserves the comparative force of meliora, which is central to the argument that Christians have superior shows.
Uses the glossary English for uoluptas, which the brief requires, and keeps the plural to match the source.
Renders the reflexive verb literally, preserving the sense of gathering oneself back from distraction, which fits the moral argument.

choices.english: the glittering choirs of the stars
choices.why: Keeps the poetic image of stars as a dancing chorus, which is the literal sense of choros and important to the passage's rhetorical elevation.

choices.english: the crests of the mountains are higher
choices.why: Renders cristae literally as 'crests' to preserve the visual comparison between theater stonework and mountain ridges.
rejected: the ridges of the mountains are higher
the peaks of the mountains are higher

choices.english: from the height of his nobility
choices.why: Keeps the spatial metaphor of culmen ('height, summit') and the literal sense of generositas as noble birth, which ties to the preceding 'son of God'.
rejected: from the summit of his high birth
from the peak of his nobility

pass_b_english: A Christian has better public shows, if he wants them. He has true and profitable pleasures, if he recollects himself. And to pass over those things he cannot yet contemplate, he has this beauty of the world to see and admire. Let him watch the sunrise, and again the sunset, as day and night return in turn. Let him watch the moon's orb marking the seasons' course by its waxing and waning, the glittering choirs of the stars shining constantly from their swift motion, the parts of the whole year divided in turn, the days themselves and nights arranged by the spaces of hours, the mass of the earth poised with its mountains, the rivers pouring forth with their springs, the seas stretched out with their waves and shores, and the air spread between, constant in its perfect harmony and bonds of concord, quickening all things by its fineness—now pouring down rain from gathered clouds, now bringing back clear weather with restored openness. And in all these things, their own inhabitants: the bird in the air, the fish in the water, the human being on the earth. These, I say, and other works of God, are the public shows for faithful Christians. What theater built by human hands can compare with these works? However great the masses of stone with which it is built, the crests of the mountains are higher. However much its gilded ceilings gleam, they will be surpassed by the brightness of the stars. No one will ever admire human works who recognizes himself as a son of God. He casts himself down from the height of his nobility who can admire anything after God.
